questions.prompt: A team reports that their model executes correctly on CPU but produces mismatched tensor shapes and silent numerical corruption when switched to a GPU backend because some operators silently default to a different memory layout (such as NCHW versus NHWC). Which of the three fundamental framework problems does this failure most directly expose?

options.label: The hardware abstraction problem, because one unified model interface must preserve consistent semantic behavior, memory layouts, and numerical behavior across diverse hardware backends
The execution problem, because the operators were evaluated eagerly instead of being captured into a static graph
The differentiation problem, because the backward pass failed to save the tensors needed by the layout conversion
The scheduling problem, because the framework placed the layout conversion after the kernel launch

questions.explanation: The failure is semantic: the same model text produced different behavior on a different backend. Preserving meaning across hardware targets is precisely the hardware abstraction problem; layout is one of the assumptions each abstraction rung must check at its boundary.

questions.prompt: A GPU performance profile reveals that a sequence of LayerNorm, dropout, and GELU activation operations each finish in microseconds, yet the device is idle most of the wall-clock step. Under the dispatch overhead law, what is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.label: The operations are arithmetic-bound: their FLOP count is too high for the accelerator's peak
The workload is overhead-bound: the fixed per-op dispatch and launch cost multiplied by the op count exceeds the device's compute-plus-memory time, so the ratio R sits above 1
The workload is bandwidth-bound: the tensors are too large to fit in cache
The GPU is thermally throttling between kernel launches

questions.explanation: Each kernel finishes fast but the gaps between them are host issue time. R = N_op * o / (t_compute + t_memory) > 1 means the host, not the device, sets the step time - the fix is fewer or cheaper dispatches (fusion, capture), or more work per dispatch (bigger batch).

questions.prompt: For a neural network with N = 10^7 parameters and a single scalar loss output M = 1, why is reverse-mode automatic differentiation the only tractable choice?

options.label: Reverse mode requires only a single forward pass to produce every gradient, while forward mode would need ~N sweeps - and neither materializes the Jacobian
Reverse mode computes numerically exact gradients while forward mode produces only approximations
Forward mode cannot handle neural networks with more than one hidden layer
Reverse mode eliminates the need to save any forward activations

questions.explanation: Forward mode carries one derivative direction per sweep: N sweeps for N parameters. Reverse mode sweeps once backward from the scalar loss, computing vector-Jacobian products for every parameter at a small constant multiple of forward cost. Its price is exactly the saved forward state the chapter prices separately.

questions.prompt: A PyTorch user modifies an intermediate activation tensor using an in-place operation (`x.relu_()`) and later sees a version-counter or 'saved tensor' error during `backward()`. What went wrong at the framework level?

options.label: In-place operations are incompatible with GPU kernels and always corrupt device memory
The in-place write mutated a value that a registered backward rule expected to read from the recorded tape, so autograd detected the version change and refused a silently wrong gradient
The tensor's strides became negative, invalidating the computation graph
In-place operations allocate a second tape that collides with the first

questions.explanation: The tape is a contract: backward rules read the forward values they recorded. In-place mutation breaks that contract - the error is autograd defending gradient correctness, and it is why the recorded program is a hazard surface, not just an optimization target.

questions.prompt: An engineering team is architecting a new commercial computer vision system. In the chapter's decision framework, what is the correct FIRST filter when choosing a framework?

options.label: Pick the framework with the largest model zoo and community
Eliminate frameworks that cannot export every required operator to a runtime fitting the deployment target, before comparing ergonomics or benchmarks
Benchmark candidate frameworks on a standard model like ResNet-50 and pick the fastest
Choose whichever framework the most senior engineer already knows

questions.explanation: Selection is triage: deployment constraints eliminate, then team pipeline and migration cost rank the survivors. A framework that cannot reach the target runtime fails regardless of ergonomics - and the deployment check is cheaper made first.

questions.prompt: True or False: When eager fallback is enabled in `torch.compile`, encountering a graph break necessarily means the compilation failed and the whole model runs slower than pure eager.

options.label: True - a graph break discards all captured work
False - a break splits the model into compiled regions and an eager remainder; the compiled regions still get fusion and scheduling, though each break forfeits cross-boundary optimization

questions.explanation: Graph-capture JIT compiles what it can hold and falls back for the rest. The real cost model is break frequency: each boundary loses the optimizations that would have crossed it, so many breaks can make the captured remainder not worth the compile time.

questions.prompt: A product manager asks: 'The model is identical - same weights, same architecture. Why does it matter which framework or mode we run it in?' Explain why 'the model is the same' does not mean 'the runtime is the same,' using the GPT-2 XL decode-step numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: The model fixes only the operation count and the weight bytes. One batch-one decode step must read ~3 GB of weights - ~0.9 ms of device work. But an eager framework issues the step as ~576 kernel launches: ~2.9 ms of launch overhead plus Python dispatch brings host issue time to ~8.6 ms, roughly 10x the device work. Same model, same math, 10x different step time - because the framework decides whether the host or the accelerator sets the pace. Fusion, capture, and export are all ways to move the step's limit from software issue back to silicon.

questions.prompt: On a whiteboard, explain to a new teammate what the autograd 'tape' is, why ResNet-50's training peak is ~100x its weight storage, and what activation checkpointing trades.
questions.modelAnswer: During forward, every op records a backward rule plus the input values that rule will need - a recorded program called the tape. Backward replays it in reverse, reading the saved values. The retention is the bill: each of L layers holds ~k tensors of batch x shape activations, so saved state grows linearly in batch and depth and peaks exactly where forward ends. ResNet-50 has only ~102 MB of weights (plus ~204 MB of Adam moments) but an 8.4-12.4 GB training peak at batch 64 - the mountain is activations. Checkpointing records a segment boundary instead of the segment's tensors, then re-runs that segment during backward: it trades a second forward's compute for a smaller live peak.

questions.prompt: A training step dispatches 200 operations at ~15 us host cost each. The modeled device time is t_compute + t_memory = 1.5 ms. (a) Compute the overhead ratio R. (b) Is the step overhead-bound? (c) What fraction of step time is dispatch? (d) Name two levers and which term of R each one moves.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) R = 200 x 15 us / 1500 us = 3000/1500 = 2. (b) Yes - R > 1, the host outruns the device. (c) Share = R/(1+R) = 2/3 ≈ 67%. (d) Fusion or capture shrinks N_op; graph replay or a leaner dispatcher shrinks o; a larger batch or bigger kernels grows the denominator t_compute + t_memory.

questions.prompt: A chain of k = 4 elementwise ops runs over an N = 1M-element FP32 tensor. (a) Unfused traffic in MB? (b) Fused traffic? (c) The traffic ratio? (d) Beyond traffic, what else does fusion remove?
questions.modelAnswer: (a) 2kNB = 2 x 4 x 1M x 4 B = 32 MB. (b) 2NB = 8 MB. (c) 4x. (d) k - 1 = 3 kernel launches plus their dispatch costs - the latency-term saving is separate from the memory-term saving, and at small N the launches can matter more than the traffic.

questions.prompt: Compiling a serving model takes 300 s once and saves 20 ms per request. Development is frozen (D = 0). (a) How many production requests break even? (b) The same model in a research loop recompiles every one of 50 iterations - how many requests now? (c) What does this say about where compile belongs in the dev/deploy split?
questions.modelAnswer: (a) N = T_compile / saving = 300 s / 0.02 s = 15,000 requests. (b) Setup cost = 51 x 300 = 15,300 s, so N = 765,000 requests. (c) Compilation is a serving investment: freeze the artifact at the deployment boundary and let the research loop stay eager. A team that compiles the experiment pays ~50x the setup for the same per-run saving.
